land.text: the Uganda Protectorate, held in Cliopatria's British East Africa shape (1961-1968) with Kenya, Rhodesia, Nyasaland, Basutoland and others

predecessors.note: Cliopatria relabels British Africa as 'British East Africa' for 1961-1972 and keeps Uganda inside its 2.68 M km2 shape until 1968, a year-range overlap with Uganda's own shape from 1963. The Kingdoms of Buganda, Bunyoro, Ankole and Toro lay inside the protectorate; the page says the 1967 constitution 'abolished the traditional kingdoms'.

capitals.name: Kampala
capitals.note: Infobox 'Capital and largest city: Kampala'. The page gives no date for the seat and mentions Entebbe only as 'the nearby city of Entebbe' with its airport, so 'from' is the start year (a bridging judgement).

correction.text: Uganda as it stands in Cliopatria's 1963 shape, applied from independence: 'Uganda gained independence from the UK on 9 October 1962'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's row begins in 1963 but independence was 9 October 1962 (infobox 'Dominion: 9 October 1962'). The shape is the 1963 one unchanged.

210,012 km2 against the infobox 241,038 km2 total (15.39 percent water, about 203,900 km2 of land): ratio 0.87 of the total, 1.03 of the land. The page mentions no border change or dispute after 1962 (not Migingo Island, not the Kagera Salient), so one shape holds for 1963-2023; the 1978 Kagera annexation and the Congo-war stay are ledger events outside it. Cliopatria's 'Republic' label starts in 1963 as the infobox does ('Republic declared: 9 October 1963'); the body text disagrees (see the rename event).
Same outline and area (210,012 km2) as 1963-2023; nothing on the page changes the territory in 2024.

region.text: Uganda: 'Uganda gained independence from the UK on 9 October 1962'

ledger.note: 9 October 1962: Uganda becomes independent of the United Kingdom as a dominion, with Milton Obote as the first prime minister. Infobox 'Dominion: 9 October 1962'. The page names the country, not a boundary.

9 October 1963: Uganda is declared a republic (infobox 'Republic declared: 9 October 1963'). The page contradicts itself: the body says the country 'would not officially proclaim itself a republic until the 1966 crisis' and that 'In 1967, a new constitution proclaimed Uganda a republic and abolished the traditional kingdoms'. Same state and land (rule 2); the infobox date matches Cliopatria's name change.

region.text: the Kagera Salient, 'a 720 square miles (1,900 km2) stretch of land between the official border and the Kagera River'

ledger.note: 30 October 1978: Uganda invades the Kagera Salient of Tanzania. 'On 30 October, approximately 3,000 Ugandan troops invaded Tanzania along four routes'; 'On 1 November, Radio Uganda announced the "liberation" of the Kagera Salient' and Ugandan media 'declared the annexation of the Kagera Salient'. Shown hatched, not as a gain: the annexation was declared, not held; Amin announced a withdrawal on 14 November and Tanzania called it 'a complete lie'.

region.text: the Kagera Salient, 'a 720 square miles (1,900 km2) stretch of land between the official border and the Kagera River'

ledger.note: Early January 1979: the last Ugandan troops leave Kagera. 'On 23 November, three TPDF brigades crossed the pontoon bridge and began reoccupying the Kagera Salient'; 'By early January, all Ugandan troops had been ejected from Kagera' (the page's sentence has no year; it follows the November 1978 events).

region.text: southern Uganda from the border at Kikagati and Mutukula to Masaka (23 February 1979), Mbarara (25 February) and Kampala (11 April 1979)

ledger.note: 20-21 January 1979: Tanzanian troops cross into Uganda. 'Tanzanian-led troops occupied some minor border settlements near Kikagati on 20 January 1979'; the Southern Brigade 'finally crossed the border on the night of 21 January and attacked Mutukula'; the offensive 'launched in mid-February' took Masaka and Mbarara. The zone is the researcher's reading of the axis to Kampala.

region.text: southern Uganda from the border at Kikagati and Mutukula to Masaka (23 February 1979), Mbarara (25 February) and Kampala (11 April 1979)

ledger.note: 11 April 1979: Kampala falls and Amin's rule ends. 'On 10 April a combined TPDF-UNLF force attacked Kampala, and secured it the following day'; 'On 13 April Lule was flown into the city and installed as the new President of Uganda'.

region.text: 'the TPDF occupied Uganda, facing only scattered resistance'

ledger.note: April 1979: Tanzanian forces hold Uganda behind the new UNLF government. 'In the following months, the TPDF occupied Uganda, facing only scattered resistance.' Hatched, not annexed (the UNLF government 'was quickly recognised by other states as the legitimate authority').

region.text: 'the TPDF occupied Uganda, facing only scattered resistance'

ledger.note: June 1979: the war ends. 'It secured the Uganda–Sudan border in June, bringing the war to an end' (infobox end '3 June 1979'). The page is silent on when the Tanzanian forces withdrew from Uganda, so this end is the end of the war, a bridging judgement; a gap-filler should open a page on the Ugandan Bush War or Tanzania's withdrawal.

region.text: north-eastern and northern Congo: Kisangani, which 'fell into rebel hands on 23 August' 1998, and the Equateur province of the MLC, the rebel group Uganda 'supported exclusively'

ledger.note: August 1998: the Second Congo War opens and Uganda holds the north and north-east of the Congo. 'It began on 2 August 1998'; 'The Tutsi-led Rwandan government allied with Uganda'; the Uganda article says the country was 'invading and occupying the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the Second Congo War'. The page gives no boundary: Orientale (Kisangani) and Equateur (the MLC) are the researcher's reading.

region.text: Kisangani, 'the diamond center', where the Ugandan and Rwandan armies clashed

ledger.note: 7 August 1999: the Ugandan and Rwandan armies fight in Kisangani. 'Tensions between Uganda and Rwanda escalated as units of the Uganda People's Defense Force and the Rwandan Patriotic Army clashed in Kisangani on the morning of 7 August'; the page's section is 1999.

region.text: Kisangani, 'the diamond center', where the Ugandan and Rwandan armies clashed

ledger.note: 17 August 1999: a ceasefire halts the first Kisangani fighting. 'The conflict lasted until 17 August, when a ceasefire was called that day.'

region.text: Kisangani, 'the diamond center', where the Ugandan and Rwandan armies clashed

ledger.note: May 2000: Uganda and Rwanda fight again in Kisangani: 'heavy fighting between Uganda and Rwanda in Kisangani in May and June 2000'.

region.text: Kisangani, 'the diamond center', where the Ugandan and Rwandan armies clashed

ledger.note: June 2000: the second Kisangani fighting ends (the page says only 'in May and June 2000'; June is the last month it names).

region.text: north-eastern and northern Congo: Kisangani, which 'fell into rebel hands on 23 August' 1998, and the Equateur province of the MLC, the rebel group Uganda 'supported exclusively'

ledger.note: 6 September 2002: the Luanda Agreement 'formalised peace between Congo and Uganda'; the year is that of the section it stands in. The page says in 2001 'Uganda and Rwanda began pulling troops back from the front line' and gives no completion date for Uganda's withdrawal, so the end is the agreement, not a dated pull-out.

southern Uganda from the border at Kikagati and Mutukula to Masaka (23 February 1979), Mbarara (25 February) and Kampala (11 April 1979)

wars.outcome: Tanzanian victory: the Kagera Salient was cleared by early January 1979, Kampala fell on 11 April 1979 and Amin fled; the infobox gives '9 October 1978 – 3 June 1979' and 'Collapse of the Second Republic of Uganda'.
wars.note: The page describes no ceasefire agreement, peace treaty or boundary change; the Moshi conference of 24-26 March 1979 is the only meeting it dates.

wars.name: Second Congo War

zones.text: north-eastern and northern Congo: Kisangani, which 'fell into rebel hands on 23 August' 1998, and the Equateur province of the MLC, the rebel group Uganda 'supported exclusively'

wars.outcome: The Luanda Agreement of 6 September 2002 'formalised peace between Congo and Uganda'; the war 'officially ended on 18 July 2003 with the establishment of the Transitional Government'.
wars.note: The page offers no territorial map text; Uganda supported the MLC exclusively and fought the Rwandan army at Kisangani in August 1999 and May-June 2000.

certainty.note: Inherited colonial boundaries; the page records no change or dispute after 1962 (Lake Victoria, the Victoria Nile and Lake Albert are natural lines). The Kagera Salient claim of 30 October 1978 to early January 1979 is a short-lived exception.

notes: Cliopatria's Uganda is the modern country throughout; no page opened shows a change of its outline after 1962, so the border moves are two short events outside the shape (Kagera 1978, the Congo 1998-2002) plus the 1962 start. Page budget: 1-2 pages; the Uganda–Tanzania War page is the second, and the Second Congo War page is shared with the Rwanda and Burundi dossiers (a third page for Uganda, because the Congo stay is Uganda's largest border event). Conflicts: the republic date (infobox 9 October 1963, body 1966/1967); the page does not date the end of the Tanzanian stay in Uganda (confidence 1). Internal changes on the page that are not Uganda's border: the 'lost counties' restored to Bunyoro after 1964 and the 1967 abolition of the kingdoms. Gazetteer name wanted: 'Kagera Salient' (the 1,900 km2 strip between the 1 degree South border and the Kagera River in Tanzania's Kagera Region). Occupation events follow the occupier's side for Kagera and the Congo (counterpart = the owner) and the owner's side for the Tanzanian stay in Uganda; the Tanzania and DR Congo dossiers should mirror them. Not opened (page budget): the Ugandan Bush War, the First Congo War (1996-97), Migingo Island.
